must_remember: The total mass of a stable nucleus is always less than the sum of the rest masses of its individual unbound constituent nucleons.
Mass defect is given by $\Delta m = [Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n] - M$ for nuclear mass, or using neutral atomic masses as $\Delta m = [Z m(^1H) + (A - Z) m_n] - m(^AZ)$.
Einstein's mass-energy equivalence relates binding energy as $BE = \Delta m \cdot c^2$, with $1\text{ u} \approx 931.5\text{ MeV}$.
Binding energy per nucleon ($\bar{B} = BE / A$) peaks around $A \approx 56$ (Iron region) with an average value of approximately $8.5\text{ MeV/nucleon}$.
The semi-empirical mass formula incorporates five energy terms: volume, surface, Coulomb, asymmetry, and pairing energies based on the liquid drop model.

glossary.meaning: The difference between the total rest mass of separate unbound nucleons and the actual mass of the assembled nucleus.
The energy equivalent of the mass defect representing the work done by attractive nuclear forces to form a nucleus.
The total binding energy divided by the mass number $A$, serving as a primary measure of nuclear stability.
Weizsäcker's formula expressing nuclear binding energy using the liquid drop model analogy containing volume, surface, Coulomb, asymmetry, and pairing terms.
Term proportional to mass number $A$ representing the short-range saturation property of nuclear forces.
Electrostatic repulsion energy among protons that destabilizes heavy nuclei, proportional to $Z(Z-1)/A^{1/3}$.
